title: Study as worship (Mishnah Peah 1:1)
hookLine: after honoring parents, kindness and peace-making, the Mishnah says study of Torah equals them all

lines: A BOOK OPEN AT THE TABLE.
cards: Eyes closed, hands folded, words said to God: that's the usual picture of worship. Here's another. A kitchen table at night.

A book open, a pencil in the margin. Someone reads one sentence over and over, frowning, flips to a commentary, reads it again, and finally sits back with a small smile because it makes sense at last.
It doesn't look like prayer. But in Jewish tradition this counts as worship too, and one old text sets it beside all the good deeds at once.

teach.b: It's called Talmud Torah, the study of Torah. Talmud here just means learning, and Torah means the whole tradition of teaching, not only the five books.

The key text is the very first teaching in a tractate of the Mishnah called Peah, later filled out by the Talmud. That fuller version is recited every morning, in the opening blessings of the daily prayers.
In paraphrase: there are things whose fruit a person enjoys in this world, while the reward remains for the world to come. Honoring your father and mother. Acts of lovingkindness.
Coming early to the house of study. Welcoming guests. Visiting the sick.
Helping a bride. Accompanying the dead. Praying with focus.
And then the last line: and the study of Torah is equal to them all. Equal to visiting the sick? To making peace?
The Talmud explains it with a debate. Some rabbis once asked: which is greater, study or action? One said action.
Their answer: study is greater, because study leads to action. You learn what kindness asks, and then you do it. Study isn't instead of the other things.

Behind it stands an old verse: "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth, but thou shalt meditate therein day and night." Not only in a synagogue. On a bus, at a table, in bed with a book.
In this tradition, learning a line of Torah is not only preparation for worship. It is worship: time spent with God's words the way you'd spend time with someone you love.

how: Many Jews set aside time each day for Torah study, alone, with a partner or in a class, and recite Mishnah Peah 1:1 in the morning blessings as part of the daily prayers.

practice: Choose one line, a verse, a line from a book you love, a sentence someone once said to you, and say it silently, then again, slower. Which word matters most, and what does it ask of you?
Stay with it the way you'd stay with a friend, without hurrying to the next line.
